clinicalPearls: Most common benign tumour of infancy; usually absent or only a faint precursor mark at birth, then rapid proliferation over the first weeks to months.
GLUT1 immunopositivity is the diagnostic hallmark and distinguishes it from congenital haemangiomas and vascular malformations.
Follows a stereotyped natural history: proliferative phase, plateau, then slow spontaneous involution over several years.
Segmental facial lesions warrant evaluation for PHACE association; lumbosacral or perineal segmental lesions for LUMBAR/PELVIS/SACRAL associations.
Beard-distribution lesions raise concern for subglottic airway involvement presenting with biphasic stridor.
Beta-blocker therapy (propranolol) is first-line for problematic lesions; ulceration is the commonest complication and cause of pain.
Periocular lesions threaten vision through induced astigmatism, amblyopia or visual-axis occlusion.
Five or more cutaneous haemangiomas should prompt abdominal imaging to exclude hepatic involvement.
reference.pathophysiology: Infantile haemangioma is a benign proliferation of endothelial cells expressing the erythrocyte-type glucose transporter GLUT1, a marker shared with placental microvasculature. Proliferation is driven by immature endothelial and pericyte populations with upregulated angiogenic signalling (VEGF, basic fibroblast growth factor) and hypoxia-related pathways. The beta-adrenergic system modulates growth, which explains the response to beta-blockade through vasoconstriction, downregulation of angiogenic drive and promotion of endothelial apoptosis. After the proliferative phase the tumour involutes, with progressive replacement of vascular tissue by fibrofatty stroma.
additionalDifferentials: Infantile fibrosarcoma or other soft-tissue tumour
Nasal glioma or encephalocoele for midline facial lesions
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis in most cases, with serial photographic documentation of growth
Doppler ultrasound showing a high-flow, high-vessel-density soft-tissue mass
MRI for deep, segmental or syndromic lesions and airway assessment
GLUT1 immunohistochemistry on biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain
Echocardiography and aortic arch imaging if PHACE is suspected
Abdominal ultrasound for hepatic haemangiomas when five or more cutaneous lesions are present
Ophthalmology and ENT/airway review as dictated by lesion site
redFlags: Periocular location threatening the visual axis
Beard-distribution or symptomatic airway lesion with stridor
Segmental facial lesion suggesting PHACE (posterior fossa, arterial, cardiac and eye anomalies)
Multiple lesions with hepatic involvement risking high-output cardiac failure
reference.prognosis: The great majority involute spontaneously with a good cosmetic outcome, although residual telangiectasia, fibrofatty tissue or atrophic scarring may persist. Timely beta-blocker therapy improves outcomes in high-risk or function-threatening lesions.
pitfalls: Assuming all birthmarks behave alike and missing the distinction from malformations, which do not involute.
Under-appreciating rapid proliferative growth and delaying treatment of periocular or airway lesions.
Failing to investigate segmental lesions for PHACE or LUMBAR associations.
Overlooking anaemia or heart failure in extensive hepatic involvement.
Attributing persistent ulceration purely to infection rather than to the lesion itself.
references: International consensus guidance on management of infantile haemangioma
